newsitem.title: INDIA: India ministry clears Tata-Singapore airline deal.
newsitem.headline: India ministry clears Tata-Singapore airline deal.

text.p: India's Industry Ministry has approved a $600-million plan by Tata Industries and Singapore International Airlines (SIA) to set up a domestic Indian airline, the Press Trust of India (PTI) reported on Monday.

The Industry Ministry sent the plan, cleared early this month by the Foreign Investment Promotion Board (FIPB), with favourable recommendations to Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's cabinet last week, PTI said.
The plan will now go forward to the cabinet committee on foreign investment before it is taken up for consideration by the entire cabinet, PTI said.

Communist parties supporting Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's shaky 13-party coalition, as well as the Hindu nationalist opposition, objected vehemently when the FIPB approved the two-year-old plan recently.
The FIPB is a panel of senior government officials attached to the Industry Ministry which can approve foreign investment upto six billion rupees to be considered by the government.
Before the plan could be considered by Deve Gowda's cabinet, however, it had to win the approval of the Industry Ministry.
Industry Ministry officials said they cleared the plan because it was too good to hold back, PTI said.
"No good proposal, that too of such a mega nature, should be held back," it quoted Industry Ministry officials as saying.
SIA and Tata Industries Ltd submitted their proposal to launch the airline in February 1995. The Tatas planned to take a 60 percent stake, with SIA holding the rest.
Since then, the proposal has languished in the government, ensnared in a high-stakes battle over whether to permit foreign investment in the civil aviation sector.
India began opening its aviation sector as part of an economic liberalisation programme launched under then prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao in 1991.

But Civil Aviation Minister C.M. Ibrahim has fought a high-profile campaign to protect the state-owned airlines -- Indian Airlines on domestic routes and Air-India on international routes -- from foreign competition.
Ibrahim has earlier said a new civil aviation policy being drafted by the government would bar foreign firms from taking an equity stake in domestic airlines.
Ibrahim's campaign has irritated free traders in Deve Gowda's centre-left coalition. But his drive has the backing of communists, who support the government.

Currently the government reviews foreign companies' proposals on a case-by-case basis. If approved, a foreign firm can take up to a 40 percent stake in a domestic airline. Gulf Air and Kuwait Airways each have stakes in India's Jet Airways.
